title: Mathematics 1
target_note: 27 questions in 40 minutes, so about ninety seconds each. Nothing here is beyond GCSE; the difficulty is entirely in choosing the short route, and most questions have an obvious method that will not fit in the time.

questions.stem_html: Work out 3 × 1081.5 × 10−3, giving your answer in standard form.
questions.solution_html:
Divide the numbers and subtract the indices: 3 ÷ 1.5 = 2, and 8 − (−3) = 11.

So the answer is 2 × 10¹¹.

Subtracting a negative index is where this is won or lost. 8 − (−3) = 11, not 5.

traps.A: The sign of the index has been lost.
traps.D: 3 × 1.5 instead of 3 ÷ 1.5, and the index subtracted wrongly.
traps.E: The indices multiplied rather than subtracted.
traps.F: Right index, but 3 × 1.5 instead of 3 ÷ 1.5.

questions.stem_html:
Two positive integers have highest common factor 6 and lowest common multiple 180.

One of them is 30. What is the other?
questions.solution_html:
For any two positive integers, HCF × LCM = their product.

So the product is 6 × 180 = 1080, and the other number is 1080 ÷ 30 = 36.

Check: HCF(30, 36) = 6 ✓ and LCM(30, 36) = 180 ✓.

Listing multiples of 30 until one has the right HCF works and takes four times as long. The product rule is one line.

questions.stem_html: Write 0.4̉5̉ (that is, 0.454545…) as a fraction in its simplest form.
questions.solution_html:
Two digits repeat, so the denominator is 99: 0.4̉5̉ = 4599.

Divide top and bottom by 9: 511.

A repeating block of length 2 gives 99, not 100 and not 90. 90 is for one fixed digit followed by one repeating.

traps.C: 0.45 exactly, unsimplified.
traps.D: A rounding, not the exact value.
traps.E: That is 0.5 recurring.
traps.F: That is 0.45 with only the 5 recurring.

questions.stem_html:
A rectangle measures 8.2 cm by 5.6 cm, each correct to 1 decimal place.

What is the upper bound for its area, in cm2?
questions.solution_html:
To 1 d.p., 8.2 lies in [8.15, 8.25) and 5.6 in [5.55, 5.65).

The largest area uses both upper bounds: 8.25 × 5.65 = 46.6125.

The bounds are ±0.05, not ±0.1. Using 8.3 and 5.7 gives 47.31 and is the commonest slip.

traps.A: 8.2 × 5.6 — the area itself, not an upper bound.
traps.B: A rounding of the area, not a bound.
traps.C: 8.15 × 5.65: one lower bound and one upper.
traps.E: A guess between the bounds.

questions.stem_html: What is the smallest positive integer n such that 360n is a perfect cube?
questions.solution_html:
360 = 23 × 32 × 5.

For a cube every index must be a multiple of 3. The 2s are already fine; the 3s need one more, and the 5s need two more.

So n = 3 × 52 = 75, and 360 × 75 = 27000 = 303.

Trying values in turn is hopeless — the answer is the 75th one you would try. Factorise first and the whole question is three indices.

traps.A: Fixes the 3s and leaves the 5s at index 2.
traps.C: Fixes the 5s and leaves the 3s at index 2.
traps.D: 3² × 5 overshoots the 3s and undershoots the 5s.
traps.E: 2 × 5² disturbs the 2s, which were already correct.

questions.detail: Making a cube by prime factors

questions.stem_html:
A coat is reduced by 20%, and the reduced price is then cut by a further 10%. It now costs £72.

What was the original price?
questions.solution_html:
The two reductions multiply: 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72 of the original.

So the original is 72 ÷ 0.72 = £100.

The reductions are not 30% together — that would give 72 ÷ 0.7 = £102.86, which is why option E is there.

traps.A: 72 ÷ 0.9 only — one reduction reversed, not both.
traps.C: 72 × 1.2 × 1.1 — adding the percentages back on rather than dividing.
traps.E: Treating the reductions as a single 30% cut.
traps.F: A rounding of the same error.

questions.stem_html:
y is inversely proportional to x2. When x = 3, y = 8.

What is y when x = 6?
questions.solution_html:
y = kx2, and 8 = k9 gives k = 72.

At x = 6: y = 7236 = 2.

Doubling x divides y by 4, not by 2. Once you see that, the constant is never needed.

traps.A: Dividing by 8 rather than by 4.
traps.C: Treating it as inversely proportional to x, so halving y.
traps.D: No change — the proportion ignored.
traps.E: Doubling y, as though it were directly proportional.
traps.F: Multiplying by 4 instead of dividing.

questions.stem_html:
The activity of a sample halves every 4 years.

What fraction of the original activity remains after 12 years?
questions.solution_html:
12 years is three half-lives.

(12)3 = 18.

Twelve years and a four-year half-life invite dividing 12 by 2 or halving 12 — both give an answer in the list.

traps.A: Four half-lives rather than three.
traps.B: Dividing by 12, not halving three times.
traps.D: Halving 12 years and then reading off, rather than counting half-lives.
traps.E: Two half-lives.
traps.F: Dividing the 12 years by the 4-year half-life and using it directly.

questions.stem_html: Simplify x2 − 9x2 + x − 12.
questions.solution_html:
Top: x2 − 9 = (x−3)(x+3).

Bottom: x2 + x − 12 = (x−3)(x+4).

The (x−3) cancels, leaving x + 3x + 4.

Both factorisations share (x−3), which is the only reason the fraction simplifies at all. Spot that and you can skip multiplying anything out.

traps.B: Cancelling the wrong pair of brackets.
traps.C: Cancelling the x² terms, which is not allowed in a sum.
traps.D: One factor kept from each of the wrong brackets.
traps.E: Cancelling term by term rather than by factors.
traps.F: The two numerator factors swapped.

questions.stem_html:
y = 2x + 1x − 3.

Make x the subject.
questions.solution_html:
Multiply up: y(x − 3) = 2x + 1, so xy − 3y = 2x + 1.

Collect the x terms on one side: xy − 2x = 3y + 1, so x(y − 2) = 3y + 1.

Hence x = (3y + 1)/(y − 2).

The x appears on both sides after multiplying up, so it has to be factored out. Anyone who divides too early loses a term.

traps.C: Sign error when collecting: it is 3y + 1, not 3y − 1.
traps.D: The coefficients 2 and 3 have been dropped entirely.
traps.E: This is the original with x and y simply swapped.
traps.F: Sign error in the denominator: y − 2, not y + 2.

questions.detail: Changing the subject with x on both sides

questions.stem_html: How many points of intersection do the line y = x + 1 and the circle x2 + y2 = 25 have?
questions.solution_html:
Substitute: x2 + (x+1)2 = 25, so 2x2 + 2x − 24 = 0, that is x2 + x − 12 = 0.

(x+4)(x−3) = 0 gives x = −4 and x = 3: 2 points.

The discriminant alone answers it: 1 + 48 = 49 > 0, so two. No need to find the points at all.

traps.A: The discriminant is positive, so the line does cut the circle.
traps.B: One would mean a tangent; the discriminant is not zero.
traps.D: A line and a circle can meet at most twice.
traps.E: A line and a circle can meet at most twice.
traps.F: Only if the 'line' were the circle itself.

questions.stem_html:
A sequence begins 2, 7, 16, 29, … and the second differences are constant.

What is the tenth term?
questions.solution_html:
First differences: 5, 9, 13 — second difference 4, so the nth term is 2n2 + bn + c.

n = 1 gives 2 + b + c = 2; n = 2 gives 8 + 2b + c = 7. Subtracting: b = −1, so c = 1.

Tenth term: 2(100) − 10 + 1 = 191.

Extending the sequence by hand to ten terms also works and takes about a minute — half your budget for two questions. The second difference gives the leading coefficient immediately: it is half of 4.

traps.A: Leading coefficient taken as the second difference itself, not half of it.
traps.B: An arithmetic slip extending the sequence term by term.
traps.C: The ninth term.
traps.D: 2n² − n with the +1 dropped, at n = 10.
traps.F: The eleventh term.

questions.stem_html: How many pairs of positive integers (x, y) satisfy 2x + 3y < 12?
questions.solution_html:
Both are at least 1, so go through y:

y = 1: 2x < 9, so x = 1, 2, 3, 4 — four.
y = 2: 2x < 6, so x = 1, 2 — two.
y = 3: 2x < 3, so x = 1 — one.
y ≥ 4 leaves nothing.

Total 7.

'Positive' excludes zero. Allowing x or y to be 0 adds eight more and gives 15.

traps.A: Only the y = 3 case counted.
traps.C: The y = 1 cases undercounted.
traps.D: Only the y = 1 cases counted.
traps.E: The y = 3 case and one y = 2 pair dropped.

questions.stem_html:
A line passes through (2, 5) and is perpendicular to 3x + 4y = 7.

Where does it cross the x-axis?
questions.solution_html:
3x + 4y = 7 has gradient −34, so the perpendicular has gradient 43.

Through (2, 5): y − 5 = 43(x − 2).

Setting y = 0: −5 = 43(x − 2), so x − 2 = −154 and x = −74.

The negative reciprocal is 43, not −43 and not 34. Two of the wrong options come from each of those.

traps.C: Using the original gradient rather than the perpendicular one.
traps.D: The right magnitude with the sign lost.
traps.E: Solving for y = 0 but adding 15/4 instead of subtracting.
traps.F: The value of x − 2, not of x.

questions.stem_html: What is the distance between (−3, 2) and (5, −4)?
questions.solution_html:
Differences: 5 − (−3) = 8 and −4 − 2 = −6.

Distance = √82 + 62 = √100 = 10.

8 and 6 is the 3-4-5 triangle doubled. Recognising it saves the square root entirely.

traps.A: Subtracting the coordinates the wrong way round somewhere.
traps.D: √136, from using 10 and 6 as the differences.
traps.E: 8 + 6 — adding the differences rather than using Pythagoras.
traps.F: The square of the distance.

questions.stem_html:
OACB is a parallelogram with OA = a and OB = b. M is the midpoint of AC.

What is OM in terms of a and b?
questions.solution_html:
In the parallelogram, OC = a + b.

M is halfway from A to C, and AC = b, so OM = a + 12b — that is a + ½b.

D and F are the same vector, and both give the midpoint of OC — the centre of the parallelogram, not the midpoint of AC.

traps.A: That is OC, the far corner.
traps.C: a and b swapped.
traps.D: The centre of the parallelogram, which is the midpoint of OC.
traps.E: Subtracting rather than adding half of b.
traps.F: Same as D, written differently.

questions.stem_html:
A regular polygon has interior angles of 156°.

How many sides does it have?
questions.solution_html:
Each exterior angle is 180 − 156 = 24°.

Exterior angles of any polygon add to 360°, so there are 360 ÷ 24 = 15 of them.

Going via the interior-angle sum ((n−2) × 180 = 156n) gets there too and takes three times as long. The exterior angle is always the shorter route.

traps.D: The exterior angle itself, mistaken for the number of sides.

questions.detail: Interior angle to number of sides

questions.stem_html:
ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Angle ABC = 73°.

What is angle ADC?
questions.solution_html:
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°.

ABC and ADC are opposite, so ADC = 180 − 73 = 107°.

Opposite angles sum to 180°; it is the angle at the centre that is double the angle at the circumference. E is there for anyone who reaches for the wrong theorem.

traps.A: 90 − 73 — treating them as complementary.
traps.B: Equal angles would make it a rectangle-like case, not a general cyclic quadrilateral.
traps.C: Only if AC were a diameter, which is not given.
traps.E: 2 × 73 — the angle-at-the-centre theorem, which does not apply here.
traps.F: 360 − 73, the reflex angle.

questions.stem_html:
Work out the exact value of

sin 60° cos 30° + cos 60° sin 30°.
questions.solution_html:
This is sin(A + B) with A = 60° and B = 30°.

So it equals sin 90° = 1.

Substituting the exact values works: √32 × √32 + 12 × 12 = 34 + 14 = 1. Same answer, four times the writing.

traps.A: That would be sin(60° − 30°) with the signs muddled.
traps.B: sin 30° — the answer to cos60cos30 − sin60sin30 is different again.
traps.C: sin 60°, from evaluating only the first product.
traps.E: Adding the two exact values without multiplying them.
traps.F: √3, from a slip in the surd arithmetic.

questions.stem_html:
Two similar solids have surface areas in the ratio 9 : 25.

What is the ratio of their volumes?
questions.solution_html:
Areas scale as the square of the length ratio, so 9 : 25 gives lengths 3 : 5.

Volumes scale as the cube: 27 : 125.

Cubing the area ratio gives 729 : 15625, which is option F. The cube applies to the length ratio, not the area one.

traps.A: The length ratio, not the volume ratio.
traps.D: Squaring the area ratio.
traps.E: Mixing a square and a cube.
traps.F: Cubing the area ratio instead of the length ratio.

questions.stem_html:
A cuboid measures 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm.

How long is the diagonal from one corner to the opposite corner?
questions.solution_html:
Apply Pythagoras twice, or use the 3D form directly:

√32 + 42 + 122 = √9 + 16 + 144 = √169 = 13 cm.

3, 4, 12, 13 is a standard quadruple, like 3-4-5 one dimension up. Recognising it removes the arithmetic.

traps.A: The diagonal of the 3 by 4 face only.
traps.C: √(36 + 145), an arithmetic slip.
traps.D: 3 + 4 + 12 — adding the edges.
traps.E: 12², the largest square alone.
traps.F: The square of the answer — the final root not taken.

questions.stem_html:
A cone has base radius 6 cm and slant height 10 cm.

What is its curved surface area, in cm2?
questions.solution_html:
Curved surface area = πrl, with r = 6 and l = 10.

= 60π cm2.

The slant height is given, so no Pythagoras is needed. Working out the vertical height (8 cm) is a wasted step, and 48π is what you get if you then use it by mistake.

traps.A: πrl with the slant height halved.
traps.B: πr² — the base area, not the curved surface.
traps.C: Using the vertical height 8 instead of the slant height 10.
traps.D: An arithmetic slip in 6 × 10.
traps.F: πr² + πrl, the total surface area, computed wrongly.

questions.stem_html:
A metal has density 8 g/cm3.

What is the volume of a 2 kg block of it?
questions.solution_html:
Convert first: 2 kg = 2000 g.

Volume = mass ÷ density = 2000 ÷ 8 = 250 cm³.

The units are the whole question. Using 2 kg directly with a density in g/cm3 gives 0.25, which is option A and is out by a factor of a thousand.

traps.A: 2 ÷ 8 — the kilograms never converted to grams.
traps.C: 2 × 8, multiplying instead of dividing.
traps.E: The mass in grams, not the volume.
traps.F: 2000 × 8 — multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.stem_html:
The mean of five numbers is 12. One of them is removed, and the mean of the remaining four is 13.

What number was removed?
questions.solution_html:
Total of the five: 5 × 12 = 60. Total of the four: 4 × 13 = 52.

The removed number is 60 − 52 = 8.

The mean went up when the number was taken away, so the number must be below the old mean of 12. That alone rules out D, E and F.

traps.A: 13 − 12 — the difference of the means, not of the totals.
traps.C: A guess just below the original mean.
traps.D: Removing the mean itself would leave the mean unchanged.
traps.E: Removing 13 would pull the mean down, not up.
traps.F: Removing a number above the mean lowers the mean.

questions.stem_html:
A bag holds 4 red counters and 6 blue counters. Two are taken at random without replacement.

What is the probability that they are the same colour?
questions.solution_html:
Both red: 410 × 39 = 1290.

Both blue: 610 × 59 = 3090.

Total 4290 = 715.

Without replacement, so the second denominator is 9. Using 10 twice gives 1325 — option F.

traps.A: Both red only, with the second denominator wrong.
traps.C: Both blue only, roughly.
traps.D: Calculated with replacement for one colour only.
traps.F: A guess at even odds.

questions.stem_html:
Of 50 people surveyed, 30 like tea, 20 like coffee and 8 like both.

A person who likes tea is chosen at random. What is the probability that they also like coffee?
questions.solution_html:
Conditioning on tea restricts us to those 30 people.

Of them, 8 also like coffee: 830 = 415.

The denominator is 30, not 50. Dividing by 50 gives 425 — option A — which is the probability of liking both, not the conditional probability.

traps.A: 8/50: the probability of liking both, not the conditional probability.
traps.C: A rounding of 4/15.
traps.D: 8/20 — conditioned on coffee instead of tea.
traps.E: A guess.
traps.F: 30/50, the probability of liking tea at all.

questions.stem_html:
Two fair six-sided dice are rolled.

What is the probability that the product of the scores is a multiple of 6?
questions.solution_html:
Of the 36 equally likely outcomes, count those whose product is divisible by 6.

A quick way: the product needs a factor 2 and a factor 3. Listing by the first die and counting gives 15 outcomes.

1536 = 512.

It is not just 'one die shows a 6'. (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 3) and several others qualify, which is why the answer is well above 16.

traps.A: The probability that a chosen die shows a 6.
traps.B: Nine outcomes, usually only those with a 6 or a (2,3) pair.
traps.C: Twelve outcomes — three of the qualifying pairs missed.
traps.E: Eighteen outcomes, over-counting.
traps.F: Twenty-one outcomes, counting multiples of 2 or 3 rather than of 6.
